title: Cokedale Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Cokedale wells have a 218-foot median depth, with finished well costs commonly estimated at $13,600-$24,000.
h1: Cokedale, Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
Buying land in Cokedale means dealing with a plains setting where well records point to a wide range of drilling conditions. Within 5 miles, Colorado DWR records show 517 permitted wells, including 399 recorded as constructed. Only 161 report a total depth, 39 report a pump yield, and 8 report a static water level, so the local data is useful but not complete.

The practical picture is a median well depth of 218 feet, a median reported yield of 3.5 gallons per minute, and a median static water level of 78 feet. Those figures help with early budgeting, but a neighboring well is not a guarantee for your lot. Ground conditions, fracture locations, casing, grout, and the intended use still need to be evaluated.

sections.heading: Cokedale well depths vary across the plains
sections.html:
The median reported depth near Cokedale is 218 feet. The middle half of recorded wells falls from 100 to 395 feet, while the 90th percentile reaches 580 feet. The deepest well in the records is 1,000 feet. That spread matters when requesting a drilling bid: a quote based only on the median may not cover a deeper hole on a difficult parcel.

Depth records show 22% of wells under 100 feet, 39% between 100 and 300 feet, 29% between 300 and 600 feet, and 10% at 600 feet or deeper. The permits mostly identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with 512 wells in that category. Fractured rock can be unpredictable because productive water-bearing fractures are not evenly distributed.

sections.heading: Reported well yield is usually modest
sections.html:
Among the 39 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 3.5 gallons per minute. The middle half runs from 1.5 to 7.0 gallons per minute. Forty-four percent report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, while 41% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute. Ten percent are under 1 gallon per minute, and 5% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

For a buyer, the 10% under 1 gallon per minute is the warning group. That may still support a carefully managed household with storage, but it gives less margin for irrigation or other demand. Ask for the well completion report, pumping test information, storage capacity, and the permitted use. Domestic and household wells make up 36% of the recorded use mix.

sections.heading: Water levels are recorded, but the trend is unclear
sections.html:
The 8 reported static water levels have a median depth to water of 78 feet. The middle half ranges from 35 to 169 feet below ground. This is useful for planning pump-setting depth and discussing construction, but it is not a complete groundwater trend for Cokedale.

Permit activity is heavily concentrated in later decades, with 262 permits in the 2010s compared with 108 in the 1990s and 57 in the 2000s. The record includes 7 permits in the 2020s and the newest permit year is 2025. Because only 8 wells report static levels and the facts do not provide a decade-by-decade water-level series, these records do not establish that the water table is dropping or stable.

sections.heading: Cokedale permit history shows who has been drilling
sections.html:
Cokedale has a long permit record, but activity increased sharply in recent decades. The records list 6 permits in the 1950s, 4 in the 1960s, 8 in the 1970s, 11 in the 1980s, 108 in the 1990s, 57 in the 2000s, 262 in the 2010s, and 7 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most active names in these records are Boday Well Drilling, associated with Alex Boday on 57 wells and Kathleen Boday on 36 wells, followed by Grande Pump Service & Ojo Sprgs Drlng &, associated with William M. Grande on 15 wells. Treat that history as a starting point, not a quality ranking. Check current licensing, references, insurance, and what the contractor includes in the bid.

sections.heading: What a new Cokedale well may cost
sections.html:
The local cost model assumes alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. The typical drilling rate is $35 to $55 per foot. At the 218-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $7,600 to $12,000. That is the hole only, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $13,600 to $24,000 at the median depth. A deeper-than-median hole can move the total upward, and the bid may also change with access, casing, grout, pump size, water testing, or difficult ground. Ask the driller to separate footage, casing, grout, pump equipment, trenching, electrical, testing, and any failed-hole terms.

sections.heading: Check water quality, septic layout, and buildability
sections.html:
Mapped environmental information deserves attention before buying. Within about 10 miles, the records show 207 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 231 historic mine features. There are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped sites do not prove that a particular well is contaminated, but they are reasons to test existing water and understand nearby land uses, mine history, and groundwater direction.

Low yield and dry holes are separate risks from water quality. Review nearby completion reports, confirm the permitted use with Colorado DWR, and have a contractor evaluate access for a rig. Septic placement, well setbacks, drainage, and the house site need to work together. A new household well may also require attention to exempt-well rules, pumping limits, and augmentation requirements in an over-appropriated basin.

sections.heading: Use nearby records before choosing a Cokedale lot
sections.html:
Start with wells closest to the parcel, then compare records from Valdez, Jansen, Starkville, Segundo, Trinidad, and El Moro. Look for depth, reported yield, static water level, aquifer description, construction details, and the age of each permit. The Cokedale data shows why several comparisons matter: wells range from under 100 feet to 1,000 feet, and reported yields range from under 1 gallon per minute to more than 15 gallons per minute.

Before closing, make the well a due-diligence item. Obtain the permit and completion report, inspect the equipment, test the water, and ask a driller for a site-specific opinion and written price assumptions. If building, confirm the well permit, septic feasibility, driveway access, power route, and intended household demand before committing to the lot.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Cokedale, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth near Cokedale is 218 feet. The middle half runs from 100 to 395 feet, but the range is broad: 22% are under 100 feet, 29% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 10% are 600 feet or deeper. The deepest recorded well is 1,000 feet.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Cokedale?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 218-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $7,600 to $12,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $13,600 to $24,000. Access, ground conditions, and final equipment can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Cokedale wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 39 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 3.5 gallons per minute and the middle half is 1.5 to 7.0 gallons per minute. Ten percent report under 1 gallon per minute. Ask for a pumping test and storage details, because a reported yield does not guarantee the same result on another parcel.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Cokedale?
faq.a: The map includes 207 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 231 historic mine features within about 10 miles. That does not establish contamination in a particular well, and there are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the actual well for appropriate contaminants, especially before relying on it for household drinking water.

faq.q: Are Cokedale wells running out of water?
faq.a: The available records do not prove a falling or stable water table. Only 8 wells report static water levels; their median depth to water is 78 feet, with a middle half from 35 to 169 feet. Review nearby records and obtain a current measurement or pumping test rather than assuming the regional figures predict your lot.
